explain.title: Why scientists use SI units
explain.body: SI units are standard units used internationally. They make it easier for scientists to share, compare and verify measurements. The system is based on 10, so conversions are convenient.

explain.title: Five base units used in chemistry
explain.body: The five are metre (m) for length, second (s) for time, mole (mol) for amount of substance, kilogram (kg) for mass and kelvin (K) for temperature.

explain.title: Derived units and prefixes
explain.body: Derived units are formed from base units. The section lists volume in m³, density in kg m⁻³ and area in m². Prefixes show multiples or fractions of a unit: kilo means 10³, deci 10⁻¹ and milli 10⁻³.

explain.title: Practical laboratory units
explain.body: Chemistry often deals with small quantities, so grams are manageable for mass and cubic centimetres (cm³) are practical for small volumes. Celsius is often convenient for temperature; the section gives K = °C + 273 for conversion to kelvin.

mistakes: Writing Kg or KG instead of kg; symbols have the correct capitalisation and are not pluralised.
Mixing up base units and derived units, such as calling m³ a base unit.
Using kilogram or cubic metre automatically for small laboratory quantities instead of explaining why grams and cm³ are practical.
Giving a prefix's name but the wrong power of ten, especially confusing milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶), nano (10⁻⁹) and pico (10⁻¹²).
For Celsius-to-kelvin conversion, forgetting to add 273 or giving the answer without the unit K.

explain.title: Error in measurement
explain.body: An error may be defined as the difference between the measured value and the actual value. Errors can happen because an instrument has limitations or because of the skill of the person measuring.

explain.title: Systematic error
explain.body: “Systematic errors may be removed by adding or subtracting a constant adjustment given to each measurement.” These errors affect accuracy. For example, an instrument may deliver a volume slightly different from the volume shown by its graduations.

explain.title: Random error
explain.body: “Random error causes one measurement to differ slightly from the next measurement.” It comes from unpredictable changes, such as environmental factors or slight changes in procedure, and often determines precision.

explain.title: The goal of measurement
explain.body: Experiments aim to produce results that are both accurate and precise. Accuracy concerns the actual value; precision concerns the consistency of repeated measurements.

mistakes: Do not confuse accuracy with precision: accuracy relates to the actual value, while precision relates to agreement among repeated measurements.
Do not say that random error is removed by a constant adjustment; the section gives that correction for systematic error.
Do not describe a random error as a fixed shift; it makes one measurement differ slightly from the next.
When asked for reasons for random error, include unpredictable changes, instrument limitations, environmental factors or slight variation in procedure.

explain.title: Accuracy
explain.body: Accuracy measures how close results are to the true or known value. Compare a reading with the true value to judge accuracy.

explain.title: Precision
explain.body: The closeness of two or more measurements to each other is called precision. Compare repeated readings with one another to judge precision.

explain.title: They are independent
explain.body: Precision is independent of accuracy. Repeated results may agree closely but still be far from the true value; a set of results may also be near the true value but spread apart.

explain.title: Classifying measurements
explain.body: Check two things separately: how close the readings are to the true value, and how close the readings are to each other. Then name accuracy and precision separately.

mistakes: Do not call repeated identical readings accurate unless they are also close to the true or known value.
Do not mix up the meanings: accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness among measurements.
Do not assume that an accurate result must also be precise, or that a precise result must also be accurate.
When classifying a set of readings, state both properties rather than only saying “good measurements.”

explain.title: SI is a shared measurement system
explain.body: SI units provide a common way to measure and communicate quantities. Their decimal prefixes make conversions straightforward. In Chemistry, litre and smaller units are often practical for liquid volumes and small samples.

explain.title: Base and derived units
explain.body: Basic SI units include metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, kelvin (K) for temperature and mole (mol) for amount of substance. Derived units are made by combining base units: area may be measured in m², volume in m³, and density in kg/m³.

explain.title: Accuracy and precision are different
explain.body: Accuracy tells how close a result is to the true value. Precision tells how close repeated measurements are to one another. A result can be precise without being accurate.

explain.title: Measurement errors
explain.body: A systematic error shifts results consistently, often because of instrument bias or a faulty method, and it affects accuracy. A random error varies unpredictably between readings. Calibration, checking zero and using a suitable technique can reduce systematic errors.

explain.title: Standard units support reliable work
explain.body: Using the same units helps people compare results, share measurements and avoid confusion. In daily life and space exploration, unit misunderstandings or conversion errors can cause serious problems.

mistakes: Do not confuse accuracy (closeness to the true value) with precision (agreement among repeated readings).
Use the correct symbol and letter case: kilogram is kg, kelvin is K, and kilo as a prefix is k.
In scientific notation, the first number must be at least 1 and less than 10; 0.000840 = 8.40 × 10⁻⁴.
Do not omit the unit from a numerical answer. Celsius-to-kelvin answers must be given in K.
Do not claim systematic errors are random: systematic errors shift readings consistently, while random errors vary unpredictably.
When explaining the benefit of SI, give a reason such as easier comparison, communication, conversion or fewer mistakes.

notes.title: SI Units in Chemistry
notes.answer: SI units are standard units that make scientific measurements easier to communicate, compare and use. The five base units used in chemistry are metre (m), second (s), mole (mol), kilogram (kg) and kelvin (K).
notes.explanation: SI units are standard units used around the world. In chemistry, they help scientists share and compare measurements clearly. Smaller units such as grams and cubic centimetres are practical for the small amounts often measured in a laboratory.
notes.simple: Scientists use the same measuring units so they can understand one another's results. In chemistry, grams and cm³ are handy for small amounts.
examples: A mass of a small laboratory sample is usually easier to write in grams than in kilograms.
A small liquid volume is usually easier to measure in cm³ than in m³.
steps: Choose its SI unit: for example, mass uses kilogram (kg) and time uses second (s).
Use a suitable prefix or smaller unit when it makes a laboratory measurement more manageable.
Write the unit symbol correctly; symbols do not change in the plural form.
notes.checkQuestion: Name the SI unit of amount of substance and its symbol.
notes.checkAnswer: The five SI base units used in chemistry are metre (m), second (s), mole (mol), kilogram (kg) and kelvin (K).

notes.title: Systematic and random errors
notes.answer: Systematic error affects accuracy; random error causes measurements to differ slightly and often determines precision.
notes.explanation: A systematic error shifts measurements in a consistent way and affects accuracy. A random error makes repeated measurements differ slightly and often affects precision. Systematic errors can be corrected by applying a constant adjustment.
notes.simple: Systematic error is a consistent measurement shift. Random error is a small, unpredictable change between measurements.
examples: If a measuring cylinder delivers slightly more liquid than its scale indicates each time, it has a systematic error.
If a student reads a measuring cylinder from a different angle each time, the readings may vary because of random error.
steps: Check whether the measurements are shifted consistently or vary unpredictably.
A consistent shift suggests a systematic error; changing results suggest a random error.
For a systematic error, apply the constant adjustment given to each measurement.
notes.checkQuestion: A student reads a measuring cylinder from a different angle each time. What type of error may this cause, and why?
notes.checkAnswer: It is a random error because the reading changes when the student views the cylinder from different angles.

notes.title: Accuracy and Precision
notes.answer: They are precise but not accurate.
notes.explanation: Accuracy tells how close a measurement is to the true value. Precision tells how close repeated measurements are to one another. A result can be precise without being accurate, or accurate without being precise.
notes.simple: Accuracy means close to the true value. Precision means repeated results are close to each other.
examples: True value: 5.0 g; repeated readings: 5.2 g, 5.2 g, 5.2 g. These readings are precise but not accurate.
True value: 20 g; readings: 19.8 g, 20.5 g, 19.6 g. These readings are more accurate overall but not precise.
steps: Find the true or known value.
Check whether each reading is close to that true value. This tells you about accuracy.
Compare the readings with one another. If they are close together, they are precise.
notes.checkQuestion: A true mass is 10 g. A student gets 11.2 g every time. Are the readings precise, accurate, both, or neither?
notes.checkAnswer: The readings are precise but not accurate.

notes.title: Measuring consistently with SI units
notes.answer: Use SI units and check measurements for both accuracy and precision.
notes.explanation: SI units give people a shared, decimal-based way to record measurements. Good measurements should be both accurate (close to the true value) and precise (consistent when repeated). Systematic errors shift measurements in a regular way; random errors cause unpredictable variation.
notes.simple: Use the same standard units so measurements can be compared. Check both whether a result is close to the true value and whether repeated results agree.
examples: A length of 2 metres can be written as 200 centimetres using a decimal conversion.
If repeated readings are close together but far from the true value, they are precise but inaccurate.
steps: Choose the appropriate standard unit for the quantity.
Record the measurement with its unit.
Repeat measurements when needed and compare the results.
Check for systematic causes, such as an incorrectly calibrated instrument.
Use suitable SI prefixes or derived units when they make the measurement clearer.

quiz.stem: Which feature of measurement is affected by systematic error?
options: It makes every result identical to the actual value
It affects the accuracy of measurements
It only changes the unit used
rationales: A systematic error does not necessarily make results equal to the actual value.
This is correct: systematic error affects accuracy.
Systematic error is not simply a change of unit.
It does not always increase precision; the section links it to accuracy.

quiz.stem: What is a random error most likely to cause?
options: A fixed error caused by a constant instrument adjustment
A small difference from one measurement to the next
The actual value of a quantity
A correction made to the instrument
rationales: A fixed error is more characteristic of systematic error.
This is correct: random error can make one measurement differ slightly from the next.
A random error is not the actual value of a quantity.
A correction is a way to address systematic error, not what random error means.

quiz.stem: Which example from measurement is most likely to produce random error?
options: The measuring cylinder is read from a different angle each time
The same fixed adjustment is needed for every reading
A scale has a consistent offset
A pipette always delivers slightly less than its marked volume
rationales: This is correct: changing the reading angle can make the volume readings vary unpredictably.
A fixed adjustment indicates systematic error.
A consistent offset indicates systematic error.
Consistently delivering a different volume indicates systematic error.

quiz.stem: What is a main reason random errors occur?
options: Only the size of the actual value
A constant adjustment applied to measurements
rationales: This is correct: random error comes from unpredictable changes during an experiment.
The size of the actual value is not a stated cause of random error.
The unit's name does not cause random error.
A constant adjustment is associated with correcting systematic error.

quiz.stem: A random error often determines which feature of an experiment?
rationales: The section associates systematic error, rather than random error, with accuracy.
This is correct: a random error often determines precision.
Random error does not determine which unit is used.
The actual value is not the feature described here.

quiz.stem: Which is not listed as a main reason for random errors?
options: The use of a constant adjustment to correct a systematic error
rationales: Instrument limitations are listed as a reason for random errors.
Environmental factors are listed as a reason for random errors.
Slight variation in procedure is listed as a reason for random errors.
This is correct: applying a constant adjustment is a way to remove systematic error, not a listed cause of random error.

quiz.stem: The true length is 8 cm. A student measures it three times and records 7 cm each time. The results are:
rationales: This is wrong because all readings are close to each other, so they are precise, but they are not close to the true value.
This is correct because the readings agree with one another but differ from the true length.
This is wrong because the readings are not close to the true length.
This is wrong because the repeated readings are close to each other, so they are precise.

quiz.stem: Which term describes the closeness of two or more measurements to each other?
rationales: This is wrong because accuracy describes closeness to the true or known value.
This is correct because precision describes how close measurements are to one another.
This is wrong because a true value is the known value being measured against.
This is wrong because measurement error is the difference between a measured value and a true value.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes accuracy?
options: Measurements are close to the known value
Repeated measurements are close to one another
A measurement is written with a unit
An instrument is used more than once
rationales: This is correct because accuracy measures how close results are to the true or known value.
This is wrong because it describes precision.
This is wrong because writing a unit does not show whether a result is accurate.
This is wrong because repeating a measurement alone does not establish accuracy.

quiz.stem: Which set of readings is both accurate and reasonably precise for a true length of 12.0 cm?
options: A reading of 12.0 cm when the true length is 12.0 cm
Readings of 10.1 cm, 10.1 cm and 10.1 cm when the true length is 12.0 cm
Readings of 11.8 cm, 12.1 cm and 12.0 cm when the true length is 12.0 cm
Readings of 8 cm, 12 cm and 16 cm when the true length is 12.0 cm
rationales: This is not a set of repeated readings, so it does not show precision.
This is wrong because the readings are precise but far from the true length.
This is correct because the readings are close to the true value and fairly close to one another.
This is wrong because the readings are spread far apart and are not all close to the true value.

quiz.stem: Which statement about precision and accuracy is correct?
options: Accuracy and precision always mean the same thing
Precision depends on the true value
An accurate result must always be precise
rationales: This is wrong because the terms describe different features of measurements.
This is wrong because precision is about agreement among measurements, not closeness to the true value.
This is correct because a result may be precise but inaccurate, or accurate but not precise.
This is wrong because accuracy and precision are independent, so an accurate result need not be precise.

quiz.stem: A true mass is 20 g. A student records 19.8 g, 20.5 g and 19.6 g. These results are best described as:
options: The results are precise but not accurate
The results are accurate but not precise
The results are both accurate and precise
The results are neither accurate nor precise
rationales: This is wrong because the readings are not all close to one another, and they are close to the true value overall.
This is correct because the readings are around the true mass, but they are not close to one another.
This is wrong because the readings are not close enough to one another to be precise.
This is wrong because the readings are close to the true value overall, so they are not wholly inaccurate.

quiz.stem: Q12.1. Which of the following pairs of quantities may be measured in the same unit?
rationales: Heat and temperature have different units: joule and kelvin (or degree Celsius).
Temperature and area have different units: kelvin and square metre.
Heat and work are both forms of energy and may be measured in joules.
Length and work have different units: metre and joule.

quiz.stem: Q12.2. In which unit we usually measure the energy present in the food?
rationales: Kilojoules can express energy, but this question asks for the usual food-energy unit among the choices.
Megajoules are energy units but are not the usual unit for the energy present in food.
A calorie is the usual unit among these options for expressing the energy present in food.
The joule is an SI energy unit, but the usual food-energy unit among these choices is calorie.

quiz.stem: Q12.3. What prefix is used for 10⁻¹²?
rationales: Mega means 10⁶, not 10⁻¹².
Pico means 10⁻¹².
Giga means 10⁹, not 10⁻¹².
Tessa is not the SI prefix for 10⁻¹².

quiz.stem: Q12.4. In SI unit of pressure is expressed in:
rationales: Newton per metre is not the SI unit of pressure.
Newton per metre square is equivalent to a pascal, but Pascal is the named SI unit asked for here.
Joule is the SI unit of energy, not pressure.
Pascal is the named SI unit of pressure.

quiz.stem: Q12.5. Which symbol is used for kilogram in SI units?
rationales: K is the symbol for kelvin, not kilogram.
k is the prefix kilo, not the symbol for kilogram by itself.
Kgm is not the SI symbol for kilogram.
kg is the SI symbol for kilogram.

quiz.stem: Q12.6. What does a mole represent?
rationales: A mole represents a specific number of entities, so this is the correct choice.
Mole is a unit for amount of substance, not a unit of mass.
Mole is not a unit of volume.
Mole is not a unit of length.

quiz.stem: Q12.7. Which unit of volume should usually be used in Chemistry?
rationales: Millilitre is useful for small volumes, but the usual unit asked for here is litre.
Litre is usually used for volume in Chemistry.
Cubic centimetre is a valid volume unit, but litre is the usual choice in this question.
Cubic metre is an SI volume unit but is generally too large for usual Chemistry measurements.

quiz.stem: Q12.8. Express 0.000840 in scientific notation:
rationales: 8.40 × 10⁻³ equals 0.00840, which is ten times too large.
840 × 10⁻⁶ equals the number but is not in standard scientific notation because its coefficient is not between 1 and 10.
8.40 × 10⁻⁴ equals 0.000840 and has a coefficient between 1 and 10.
84.0 × 10⁻⁵ equals the number but is not in standard scientific notation because its coefficient is not between 1 and 10.

quiz.stem: Q12.9. In SI units prefix nano means:
rationales: Nano means 10⁻⁹.
10⁻⁸ is not the value represented by nano.
10⁻¹¹ is not the value represented by nano.
10⁻¹² is pico, not nano.

modelAnswer: SI units are based on 10, so they are easy to learn and convert.
They use definite and precise standards.
Their units are interrelated, so one unit can be derived from other units without conversion factors.
Therefore, SI units make scientific communication easier.

written.text: Compare the units in SI system with those in MKS system?
modelAnswer: SI is an internationally agreed system of units.
MKS uses metre for length, kilogram for mass and second for time.

SI includes additional base units and standard prefixes.

written.text: What are five basic SI units which are used in Chemistry?
modelAnswer: The five basic SI units used in Chemistry are:
metre (m) for length,
kilogram (kg) for mass,
second (s) for time,
kelvin (K) for temperature and mole (mol) for amount of substance.

written.text: Explain the three units derived for the basic SI units.
modelAnswer: Derived units are formed by combining basic SI units.
Area is measured in square metres (m²).
Volume is measured in cubic metres (m³).
Density is measured in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³).

Smaller units of mass and volume make these quantities easier to measure and express.

A common system of units helps avoid these difficulties.

written.text: Elaborate the difference between precision and accuracy.
modelAnswer: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value.
Precision is how close repeated measurements are to one another.
Thus, accuracy compares a result with the true value, while precision compares repeated results with each other.
A set of results may be precise but inaccurate, accurate but not precise, both, or neither.

written.text: Elaborate the importance of using SI units in space exploration.
